title: Blessings are tools (9:1)
hook: the Torah's promised rewards are means, so we can keep serving
tomorrow: if not for the reward, then why do good at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday: no body, only closeness. Maimonides' world to come is nearness to God, not a feast. Which makes one thing in the Torah look strange.

Graduation season brings the envelopes: a check from a grandparent, a laptop from an aunt, sometimes a note tucked inside that says use it well. Maimonides asks a question that turns out to be about those envelopes. If the real reward for doing good is the world to come, why does the Torah keep promising rain, peace and full barns? Isn't that a second, smaller reward?
screen: `USE IT WELL.` → `WHY PROMISE RAIN AND BARNS?` → `A SECOND REWARD?`

segments.voice: His answer: the blessings aren't the reward. They're the tools. God gave the Torah, he says, and promised that if we keep it with joy, the things that block us will be taken away: sickness, war, hunger. And the things that strengthen our hands will be given: plenty, peace, silver and gold. Why? So that people won't spend all their days on what the body needs, and will be free to learn and to do good. The full barn is a cleared afternoon. The rain is time. That's the week's question: what is a gift for? And one neighbor answers it in its own words. Christians have a line close to this. In the New Testament, the first letter of Peter says: "As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God." A steward holds something that isn't only theirs, to put it to work. The shared thread: what you've been given points past itself. And the honest difference. Peter's letter speaks of the gifts each person has received, used to serve one another. Maimonides speaks of the Torah's promised blessings, rain and peace and plenty, as room to learn and keep the commandments on the way to the world to come. Two traditions, two different books, and one instinct in common: a gift is for using.
screen: `NOT THE REWARD: THE TOOLS.` · `TAKEN AWAY: SICKNESS, WAR, HUNGER.` · `FREE TO LEARN AND DO GOOD.` · `1 PETER: GOOD STEWARDS.` · then, large: `BLESSINGS ARE TOOLS.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you that you were given or earned: a phone, a pair of shoes, the chair you're in. Keep your eyes on it for the whole sit. Ask it one question: what are you making room for? Let whatever answer comes stay with you, without deciding anything yet.
Blessings are tools: Maimonides' answer. The Torah's promised rain and peace clear the way to learn and do good.
Hold on to this: blessings are tools, and a gift points past itself. Twenty-three of thirty, carried.
